📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Uber hopes to hit 1 million daily drone deliveries by 2029.

It has been revealed that uber has grand ambitions for its drone delivery program. It's aiming to reach 1 million drone deliveries per day by 2029 after partnering with Zipline. The service is kicking off today, as Uber Eats customers in the Houston suburb of Spring, Texas, can now request drone deliveries. Dallas is the next market ahead of a broader expansion to dozens of cities across the US.

Zipline's drones can deliver orders weighing up to eight pounds as far as 10 miles away from a restaurant. Uber mentioned the drones can fly in rain and other bad weather at up to 70 mph. They lower pods containing orders into customers' yards or driveways from more than 300 feet in the air. Uber added that the drones take the quietest paths to their destinations, depending on the wind, speed and altitude.

In a recent development, uber Eats users can tap a dedicated icon on the app's home page to see restaurants that support drone deliveries. In the Houston area, the options include chains such as Jersey Mike's and Zaxby's as well as local eateries, and drone deliveries will be available from 8AM to 10PM to begin with. Users can place their order and choose a drop-off area. They'll be able to track the drone's location in real time. Uber noted that customers won't be prompted to tip for a drone delivery and nor are there any extra fees.

Recent findings suggest that rival DoorDash already offers drone deliveries in parts of Dallas–Fort Worth and Charlotte, North Carolina with the help of its partners Wing, Flytrex and Manna. DoorDash is also making its own drones and it will first offer deliveries using them in northern California.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Similar to a recent iPhone feature, Google appears to be working on “Fast Switch” as a way to share one SIM and phone number on two Android phones at once, and it sounds pretty cool.
  • Through the SIM Manager app on Android, the folks over at Android Authority noticed strings that tell a pretty clear story.
  • A new feature called “Android Fast Switch” would let you “use your phone number on up to two phones,” with the SIM automatically switching to “whichever phone you unlock.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Similar to a recent iPhone feature, Google appears to be working on “Fast Switch” as a way to share one SIM and phone number on two Android phones at once, and it sounds pretty cool.

Through the SIM Manager app on Android, the folks over at Android Authority noticed strings that tell a pretty clear story.

A new feature called “Android Fast Switch” would let you “use your phone number on up to two phones,” with the SIM automatically switching to “whichever phone you unlock.”.

“Android Fast Switch” sounds nearly identical to Handoff on iPhone, a feature that lets iPhone owners share one SIM between two iPhones and quickly switch devices on the fly.

Other strings explicitly say that you can “Use a SIM on two phones” and specify that both devices would need to be logged into the same Google account. One phone would be the “Primary” with the other as a “companion.”.

It has been revealed that there are still plenty of unknown details here, including what data might sync between devices as well as how carriers will respond. On iPhone, carriers either charge extra for this feature ($5 at T-Mobile, $10 at Verizon), or don’t support it at all (AT&T). We also don’t know what devices may be supported – this could easily end up as a Pixel-only affair.

According to recent reports, as per usual with these early teardowns, though, the actual launch of a feature like this could be weeks, months, or even years away. Still, the idea itself is rather exciting.

Sources indicate that iPhone’s Handoff feature always sounded useful, but I personally always questioned why it would be useful on iPhone. With so little variety in hardware, the utility of switching between two iPhones seems somewhat dubious, outside of perhaps using a Mini or Air as a situational device alongside a Pro device.

Sources indicate that on Android, the combinations are endless. It all just depends on what devices Google supports. What devices would you switch between?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A security researcher has discovered that some of the world’s most popular websites were compromised in an attempt to steal cryptocurrency from iPhone users.

According to recent reports, A total of 178 websites were affected, including BBC, CNN, HSBC, IKEA, and Zoom. Reasonably recent versions of iOS are safe, and so far it appears that only a few thousand dollars have been stolen ….

Reuters reports that hackers attacked Optimizely, a website optimization platform used by many major websites.

Recent findings suggest that several of the affected companies stated that they have disabled the Optimizely scripts and are investigating potential impacts. Helme says almost all of the rogue code has now been removed, and that Apple patched iOS after an identical attack method was detected last month.

In a recent development, the Coruna loader is byte-identical to a sample we analysed in October from a different campaign. The kit’s own comments say iOS 18.7.3 and later, and 26.3 and later, are patched.

Helme monitored the attacker’s wallets and discovered that only $7,040 has been stolen, though it’s not possible to see how many payment card numbers were obtained.

As always, the best protection against this type of attack is to promptly update all your Apple devices to the latest OS versions they support.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Apple doesn't give you very much iCloud storage when you purchase one of its products, and no matter how many of its devices you buy, you never get more than a stingy 5GB.
  • That space is occupied by all your photos, videos, backups, mail, mail attachments, data from apps like Messages and Notes, the contents of your iCloud Drive and some third-party app data — even images stored in Shared Albums, which began to count against your storage with iOS 27.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A few settings changes can stop your iCloud from filling up again.

Apple doesn't give you very much iCloud storage when you purchase one of its products, and no matter how many of its devices you buy, you never get more than a stingy 5GB. Since almost everything you sync or back up with Apple shares that space, how do you free up space once iCloud gets full?

That space is occupied by all your photos, videos, backups, mail, mail attachments, data from apps like Messages and Notes, the contents of your iCloud Drive and some third-party app data — even images stored in Shared Albums, which began to count against your storage with iOS 27.

Recent findings suggest that you can upgrade your iCloud subscription from just $0.99 a month for 50GB, but deleting costs nothing. You can delete data held in files, photos, app backups, voice memos and everything else, either on your Apple device or via the iCloud website. However, anything you delete will be gone after a 30-day delay. Keep in mind that anything you remove from any of your apps, including photos and videos, will disappear across all your devices.

You can check how much storage is being used and by what in iCloud Settings on your device or on the iCloud website. Go to Settings > [Your Name] > iCloud. Then click Manage (on Mac) or tap Storage (on iOS) to reach the storage management section. Note that on a Mac, Settings is called System Settings.

Here you can review a list of all the apps taking up storage space, ranked by size. You'll usually find Photos, Mail, Backups, iCloud Drive and Messages at the top of the list. It is also worth scrolling down to see if there are any apps you no longer use, taking up this precious space.

Here are five of the fastest ways to free up iCloud storage:.

Sources indicate that photos and Mail are usually the biggest space hogs, so start there. To manage your Photos, tap Photos in iCloud Settings, then Manage Storage. You'll see how many photos and videos you have synced with iCloud and find tools Apple provides to get rid of duplicates.

Another option is to transfer your iCloud photos to Google for image archiving or use an external HDD or SSD drive. iCloud Mail also counts toward your storage, so delete large attachments and empty your Trash, Junk and Deleted messages frequently.

In a recent development, one final step: check the Recently Deleted folders in Photos, Mail, iCloud Drive and Notes frequently, as these hold items for about 30 days once you delete them. This lets you rescue items you deleted by mistake, but also means your storage remains full.

If you find items you want to delete in those folders, select them and tap Delete to override the delay.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As AI-generated slop continues to flood music streaming platforms, Spotify is rolling out an “Artist Profile Protection” tool to all artists, giving them control over the music appearing under their name.
  • Spotify states the tool is designed to address a longstanding issue across streaming services, where music can end up on the wrong artist profile due to deliberate impersonation, metadata errors, or shared artist names.
  • The update comes as Billboard reported last month that Sony Music had requested the removal of more than 260,000 deepfake songs from digital platforms, nearly double the number the label disclosed in March.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As AI-generated slop continues to flood music streaming platforms, Spotify is rolling out an “Artist Profile Protection” tool to all artists, giving them control over the music appearing under their name. The official launch comes eight months after the organization began beta testing the feature with select artists.

Spotify states the tool is designed to address a longstanding issue across streaming services, where music can end up on the wrong artist profile due to deliberate impersonation, metadata errors, or shared artist names.

The update comes as Billboard reported last month that Sony Music had requested the removal of more than 260,000 deepfake songs from digital platforms, nearly double the number the label disclosed in March.

With this new feature, Spotify is aiming to give artists more control over their digital identities as the volume of music uploaded to streaming services continues to grow.

Artists can enable the feature through Spotify for Artists to receive alerts when upcoming music is submitted under their name. If a release doesn’t belong to them, they can remove their association with it to stop it from appearing on their profile.

Sources indicate that by default, releases go live as scheduled unless an artist intervenes. If artists want greater control, they can choose to switch on an advanced setting that requires them to manually approve or reject releases before they appear on their profile.

“Artists should never have to find someone else’s music under their name, noted Sam Duboff. Spotify’s Global Head of Marketing and Policy, in an email, stated to TechCrunch. “Their artist profile should be in their control. Starting today, every artist on Spotify can use Artist Profile Protection to review what reveals up on their profile and prevent spammy and incorrect releases from ever reaching their page or their fans. We’re the first and only streaming service with a solution to the industry-wide problem of content mismatch, and we hope it sets a upcoming standard for streaming platforms.”.

The company says it worked with thousands of artists during the beta testing phase to refine the tool and make it easier to protect their profiles without disrupting release schedules.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NC Band 2 is smaller, sleeker and has a longer battery life.

Recent findings suggest that natural Cycles is today announcing two upcoming products; its second-generation fertility-tracking wearable, the NC Band 2, and its first ever smart ring, the NC Ring. The former is a refinement of last year's debut model, which has been redesigned to make it easier to wear. The latter shrinks down that same technology into a ring, albeit one that isn't going to be available in the US. If you're unfamiliar, Natural Cycles made its name with its FDA-cleared health app offering "digital birth control.".

Industry observers note that let's start with the Band 2. As before, it's a screen-free band, but with a raft of fit and finish tweaks made between the first and second generations. The older unit was designed to be worn only while sleeping, monitoring the wearer's heart rate, movement and temperature. Its successor, however, is a general-purpose activity tracker which can be worn day and night, adding additional insights into its user's health.

The focus remains on fertility, and the band will interact directly with the Natural Cycles app offering personalized insights. Customers can run one of five distinct modes: Birth Control, Strategy Pregnancy, Follow Pregnancy, Postpartum and Perimenopause.

There have also been plenty of improvements to the hardware, with the Band 2 far smaller and lighter than its predecessor. Despite the smaller form factor and all-day wear, the battery life has increased from 14 days to 21. It's also a lot hardier, being able to withstand being immersed in water to depths of up to 50 meters.

The newly introduced NC Band 2 is available to pre-order today, priced at $149 alongside a year's app initiative, or $99 for existing consumers. It is HSA/FSA eligible and the company expects it to begin shipping at some point in December.

Of more interest, but not available in America, is the NC Ring, which begins shipping today in Canada, Europe and Australia. Measuring 2.43mm thick and 5.8mm wide, it's designed to keep an eye on its user's temperature and movement. It doesn't ship with an optical heart rate sensor both to reduce any night-time distractions and to keep the battery life running for up to 14 days on a charge. Like its wrist-worn siblings, it'll connect via Bluetooth to the Natural Cycles app to offer up more data for fertility and cycle tracking.

Recent findings suggest that if you're wondering why Natural Cycles isn't selling the ring in the US, your guess is as good as ours. It certainly wouldn't do to speculate as to why it would choose to ignore such a lucrative and vast market. Apropos of nothing, Natural Cycles has a longstanding partnership with market leaders Oura, itself no stranger to using its patent library to shut down potential competitors.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Isomorphic Labs, an artificial intelligence drug discovery startup founded by former Google DeepMind chief Demis Hassabis, has raised a $5 billion Series C, the tech giant stated on Tuesday.

Isomorphic's round comes three-and-a-half months after Hassabis stepped back as CEO of DeepMind, Google's AI lab, which he co-founded before the Major Tech giant acquired it in 2014.

The round was co-led by Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital, alongside Andreessen Horowitz, with investment from Alphabet, Google's parent. The fresh funds will help fund the design and development of fresh medicines using AI.

Drug discovery startups have seen record funding poured into them by investors in 2026 as companies look to capitalize on advances in AI. OpenAI and Anthropic have also been investing in tools to develop newly introduced medicines using the technology.

Hassabis has been CEO of Isomorphic Labs since the startup spun out of DeepMind in 2021.

"When we founded Isomorphic, our conviction was that biology could be understood and modelled at the most fundamental molecular level and radically accelerated through AI," remarked Hassabis.

"This round enables us to accelerate our progress: building foundational biology models, deepening our systemic disease understanding, and driving our first therapeutic programs towards clinical trials to deliver tangible impact for patients," he added.

Isomorphic is building a proprietary drug design engine and therapeutic candidate pipeline designed with AI, which it indicates will help it deliver the next generation of medicines.

Anthropic revealed it was launching an AI drug discovery program in June and OpenAI partnered with Novo Nordisk in April.

Drug discovery startups have raised $23.2 billion in 2026, according to deal-counting platform Dealroom, a record figure.

Isomorphic last raised in May, with a $2.1 billion Series B.

#741. Artist brings old Space Shuttle tank back to life

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1321 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Artist brings old Space Shuttle tank back to life

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1321 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Natalie Rosen is not the type of specialist you immediately associate with being one of the key people behind the fresh exhibit of the space shuttle Endeavour.
  • In a recent development, she is not a former NASA technician or engineer, as many of her colleagues have been for the past several years, nor is she a curator or conservator.
  • Without her expertise and artistry, however, the largest component of Endeavour‘s “stack” would look nothing like it did when the shuttle was flying.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Natalie Rosen is not the type of specialist you immediately associate with being one of the key people behind the fresh exhibit of the space shuttle Endeavour.

In a recent development, she is not a former NASA technician or engineer, as many of her colleagues have been for the past several years, nor is she a curator or conservator. Before this job, she had no experience working on any aircraft or spacecraft, as the new Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center, an extension of the California Science Center, opened in Los Angeles on November 13.

Without her expertise and artistry, however, the largest component of Endeavour‘s “stack” would look nothing like it did when the shuttle was flying.

“My background is in the fine arts. I have my bachelor’s and my master’s in fine arts from Cal State Long Beach,” Rosen told collectSPACE.com. “When I came in on this project, they were looking for a sculptor, and I had been sculpting.”.

In a recent development, rosen had been working with mixed media for her thesis project and had experience sculpting foam. As it happened, the California Science Center had a lot of foam that needed shaping.

In a recent development, for those unfamiliar, the space shuttle was assembled from three primary launch components. The orbiter and its solid rocket boosters were reusable, given the time needed to inspect, service, and, in the case of the solid-fuel motors, refurbish and refill between flights.

It has been revealed that the 154-foot-tall (47-meter) external tank was the only major part of the stack that was disposed of with each launch. After providing propellant for the orbiter’s three main engines, the tank was jettisoned and disintegrated while reentering the atmosphere.

Industry observers note that to protect the orbiter from the extreme cold of the cryogenic liquid oxygen and liquid hydrogen in the external tank and to keep the propellant and oxidizer from boiling off too swiftly, the ET was covered in insulating foam. (Some of that foam became liberated during ascent and was what caused the loss of the space shuttle Columbia and its crew in 2003.).

According to recent reports, the only flight-worthy tank to remain at the end of the program was ET-94. A so-called lightweight tank, it was built at a time when NASA was transitioning to a super-lightweight model and was therefore set aside. Originally slated to support a science mission on Columbia, it instead became a testbed after the tragedy, having its foam stripped off and tested to better understand what had happened.

It has been revealed that after the program ended, NASA donated ET-94 to the California Science Center. It arrived by way of a transoceanic barge and a road trip, then sat at Exposition Park for nearly a decade.

“So much of the foam on the ET had been dissected and removed during its time as a test article that they [the California Science Center] were trying to figure out how to put it back on and blend it in to the original foam in a convincing way,” said Rosen.

There has been a longstanding debate among shuttle enthusiasts and modelers about exactly what color the external tank is, and the answer resides in the foam.

Industry observers note that “It’s orange. It’s cream. It’s burnt sienna. It just depends on the original foam, when you’re seeing it and how it’s aging. Because it starts as a kind of very ice cream-white almost color, and then depending on how long it sits out in the Sun, it turns orange,” said Rosen.

According to recent reports, by the time she had come on staff, the decision for the most part had already been made. Dennis Jenkins, the leader of the Endeavour project, had blended a special paint called “ET Orange” that was used to cover the existing acreage “bumpy” foam. Separately, a mocha-like color was picked out for the intertank.

According to recent reports, “And then the latest foam to be installed, which would have looked the newest on all of the closeout hardware—the feed lines, the ice frost ramps, the flanges around the intertank and the intertank rings—those were all the lightest color that we custom mixed. That was what we called the ice cream color,” Rosen noted.

It was not only about color matching, though. For multiple reasons, the original aerospace-grade foam could not be used, so a commercial substitute had to be found that could match what Rosen described as the “orange peel.”.

It has been revealed that “If you look at the tank very closely, there’s this bumpy texture, and there is a pattern from the original manufacturing and how it was sprayed on. There’s this overlapping line, a subtle-like stripe to it,” she remarked.

Replicating that pattern was not easy.

“There was a lot of trial and error in the beginning of what we could do to try and get it to match what was already there,” Rosen told collectSPACE. “We tried taking impressions off of the real foam and making molds and casting, but that didn’t really work. I then suggested we put in a dense urethane, like plain urethane foam, and I hand-sculpt the top of it to match what was around it. That ended up becoming the best solution for fixing the acreage foam that had an orange peel-like texture.”.

Jenkins, who had worked as a space shuttle engineer and led NASA’s delivery of the orbiters to their museum homes, had high praise for Rosen and her work.

“She had to come up with a lot of new processes because we couldn’t apply foam the same way they did at Michoud. It’s not flightworthy by any means, but just coming up with how to make it look real took a lot of imagination on her part, and she was pretty much a one-woman show for most of it,” he noted.

Recent findings suggest that some of the repair work to the external tank was finished before it was lifted by crane into the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center and mated with the boosters and Endeavour. From then on, Rosen had to climb scaffolding to get to her worksites.

“It’s definitely the largest art project I’ve ever worked on, and, I mean, I touched every inch of it,” Rosen mentioned. “Once it went vertical, I was going up and down stairs. Probably the scariest was the point in the scaffolding where it just became ladders. So I had to be very, very careful and calculated in what I was doing.”.

Recent findings suggest that even after the scaffolding was removed in preparation for the museum opening, Rosen’s ascents were not over. A couple of weeks ago, she had to install a final component on the aft dome of the liquid hydrogen tank. To reach that, she needed a scissor lift.

According to recent reports, now that the entire Endeavour stack has made its public debut, Rosen is not parting ways with the California Science Center. Her work on ET-94 has launched her career into a new frontier.

“In this last year, I have been working on different artifacts with the team. I have been helping leading up to the opening. I’ve helped in ways with the different aircraft, with their assembly, their disassembly, and reassembly. I’ve done some repairs in certain areas. I’ve worked with our satellite and probe collection to do repairs and also contacted specialists outside of my realm to clean and repair thermal blankets,” said Rosen.

It has been revealed that “So I’m planning on staying with the museum for now. They’ve offered me another position, and I’m happy to stay,” she stated.

Sources indicate that the California Science Center’s Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center is now open to the public. Admission is free, but timed entry tickets are needed due to the high demand. Reservations can be made online or at 213-744-2019.

The same core design has been in use for over half a decade at this point, with only the smallest tweaks in the past few generations. And it’s been a problem, too. I’d say beggars can’t be choosers, but this is Samsung we’re talking about – I think it’s fair to ask for a bit more.

  • The Commerce Department stated Monday it was planning to introduce latest export controls on AI chips and data centers outside of the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia has formed a committee to oversee national security policies and export control compliance following the abrupt resignation of CEO Jensen Huang over allegations of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy who had links to one of the manufacturer’s customers.

Nvidia said Tuesday that the fresh standing committee will give board-level oversight of national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risks. The move comes amid increased scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Huang’s alleged ties to the suspected spy and his advocacy for easing restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China.

The Commerce Department stated Monday it was planning to introduce latest export controls on AI chips and data centers outside of the U.S. in an effort to prevent companies in China and elsewhere from circumventing existing rules by remotely accessing AI infrastructure located in other countries. The interim rule was made in direct response to the unfolding chip smuggling scandal at Nvidia.

The announcement comes just a few hours before Nvidia’s highly anticipated third-quarter earnings call. Analysts, the media, and shareholders expect the manufacturer to address the controversy and outline how it might affect operations. This is the first major action by the company under the leadership of Collette Kress, the company’s CFO who took over as interim CEO after Huang stepped down last week.

Recent findings suggest that the committee, which will meet at least quarterly, will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson and include fellow directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri as members.

In a recent development, nvidia already has a national security team and global trade compliance team. Those teams will now report to this board committee and Kress on day-to-day operations.

Huang has agreed to testify before Congress later this month.

#737. Router VPN vs. VPN app: How are these setups different?

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (673 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

Router VPN vs. VPN app: How are these setups different?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (673 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Should you install a VPN on your router or your devices?
  • If you're a frequent VPN user, you may have an app installed on each one of your devices.
  • But even though a router-level VPN connection sounds like a good idea, it has its own set of drawbacks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Should you install a VPN on your router or your devices?

If you're a frequent VPN user, you may have an app installed on each one of your devices. But many routers these days have built-in support for VPN connections too. In theory, this means you can simply connect your router to the VPN and route internet traffic from every connected device on your network through the encrypted tunnel.

But even though a router-level VPN connection sounds like a good idea, it has its own set of drawbacks. While it can save you from managing individual connections, routing your household's internet traffic through a VPN on your router can lead to slower speeds.

Sources indicate that having noted that, not every device supports VPN connections, so tunneling your router is often your only option. That raises an crucial question: When does it make sense to use a VPN on your router, and when are individual apps the better option?

There are good reasons to connect your router directly to a VPN instead of configuring each individual device. The first one is that you don't have to install apps on different devices, sign in to your account and remember to enable the tunnel every single time. Many of the best VPN services also restrict how many devices can connect at once. Your router takes up just one slot while routing traffic from all devices on your network through the VPN.

In a recent development, most VPN providers have dedicated apps for major operating systems including Windows, macOS, Android, iOS and even Linux. However, many devices that would benefit from a VPN connection, including game consoles like the Nintendo Switch and the PlayStation 5, don't offer support for it. Take smart TVs, for instance. Even though you might want to use a VPN for streaming apps like Netflix, many mainstream TV operating systems such as Samsung's Tizen and LG's webOS don't offer any VPN settings whatsoever. One of the ways to get around this would be to use a VPN-capable streaming device like an Nvidia Shield.

It has been revealed that finally, some routers have excellent VPN policy controls that allow you to selectively route certain website domains or devices through the encrypted tunnel. For example, you could choose to only route your smart TV's traffic or Netflix-related data through a VPN. Very few routers support this functionality, though.

Even with a router that has built-in VPN support, using a VPN directly on individual devices is often the better choice. If you mainly use a VPN to access geo-restricted content on streaming services like Netflix, or for the occasional task where connection security and privacy matter more than usual, a VPN app lets you select different locations and servers without affecting anyone else's connectivity in your household.

Many websites also block connections originating from VPN servers, which is why most people don't leave a VPN running at all times. For example, you may notice Google search often requires completing a CAPTCHA when you access it through a VPN. Other websites may fail to load entirely, leaving you with an HTTP 403 or 401 error. With a device-level connection, you can promptly disable the VPN to load a stubborn website.

Not every router is powerful enough to handle VPN encryption at high speeds. In practical terms, this means you may see a severe reduction in bandwidth with a VPN enabled on your router. Your smartphone or computer is significantly more powerful, so a device-level VPN connection can make full use of your internet connection instead of being bottlenecked to slower speeds.

It has been revealed that while using a VPN on individual devices offers these advantages, note that each device takes up one connection slot, so you may want to keep the number of simultaneous connections down to a minimum. Leaving a VPN running all the time on your phone or laptop can also lead to battery drain, but with an app, you can switch it off whenever you don't need it.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Smart glasses organization Xreal has released its magnum opus—the Xreal Aura, a $1,279 pair of extended-reality glasses that runs on Google’s Android XR platform.
  • In a recent development, the Aura glasses arrive just before the first wave of Android XR glasses from Google and Samsung, in partnership with glasses manufacturers Warby Parker and Gentle Monster.
  • Sources indicate that the first big caveat about the Aura glasses is that they’re wired.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Smart glasses organization Xreal has released its magnum opus—the Xreal Aura, a $1,279 pair of extended-reality glasses that runs on Google’s Android XR platform. The Aura glasses can project virtual screens into the wearer’s field of vision and include augmented-reality elements for use in the real world.

In a recent development, the Aura glasses arrive just before the first wave of Android XR glasses from Google and Samsung, in partnership with glasses manufacturers Warby Parker and Gentle Monster. Those devices aim squarely at Meta’s smart-glasses empire. But the Aura glasses are more like virtual reality headsets, now in a more comfortable, glasses-like design. They go head-to-head with Meta’s VR Glasses, slated for release in early 2027.

Sources indicate that the first big caveat about the Aura glasses is that they’re wired. A long cord hooks onto the end of one of the glasses’ arms via a USB-C cable. That cord connects to an attached compute puck, about the size of a smartphone and weighing a little more than a half-pound. It comes in 12 or 16 GB storage options and has a battery that powers the glasses for roughly four to five hours with constant use.

It has been revealed that when the Aura glasses work, they’re wonderful. The glasses are pretty lightweight, at 95 grams. A four-mic array sits in the arms with Bose EQ tuning that sounds great. (You can also connect wireless headphones.) The display screen has a 1920 x 1200-pixel-per-eye resolution that is noticeably better than other Xreal glasses I’ve worn. A 70-degree field of view means the screens and virtual elements pop up in a wide frame of the wearer’s vision. That means the outer edges of your view will still be the real-life room around you. That can help if you’re trying not to fall over, but it can also be noticeable when trying to feel immersed in a movie.

According to recent reports, the big thing about Aura is that you can, in theory, run every app that already exists on Android. Xreal has a few primary categories for how it expects people to use its Aura glasses. The big one is entertainment. Like other Xreal glasses, the Aura can project a screen right in your field of vision. You can watch movies, TV shows, or YouTube videos, right in your field of view. The virtual screen stays fixed, or it can follow you around as you turn your head. You can also unplug the glasses from the compute puck and use them as display glasses to extend your Steam Deck’s screen, for example, though I had issues with that when playing more graphics-intensive games like Cyberpunk 2077.

The Aura glasses attach to a compute puck for processing, which also doubles as a battery.

According to recent reports, the other massive use case is productivity. The Aura glasses can host virtual workstations that let you swap between tabs and keep multiple tasks running. So you can have a Google Doc right in front of you, Spotify to the side, and those Slack messages you keep ignoring in the back. If you’ve ever wished you had even more space to stash all your browser tabs, this is the device for you. Pair it with a Bluetooth keyboard, and you’ll have a whole workstation on your face, even on a plane, without having to crane your neck awkwardly at a laptop. I wrote almost half this review with the glasses as my screen, but eventually swapped back to a regular desktop to give my eyes a rest.

There are also augmented reality experiences, like using Google Earth to turn a room into a 3D model of a city that you can stomp around in like Godzilla, plus immersive virtual tours so you can see exotic places like the Galapagos.

Two lenses are set in the frame, one smaller lens behind the other. The smaller lens carries the display and AR elements, popping them up within a 70-degree field of view. The outer lens can go from perfectly see-through to very dark. Turning up the darkness makes it easier to see the projected virtual screens. Turning the darkness down enables a much clearer pass-through, which can help you avoid tripping over things while walking around.

According to recent reports, that stated, these glasses aren’t really meant to be worn while walking around. Even with no AR elements enabled, the double-lens layout feels distracting. There is also no way around the fact that these glasses are still pretty chunky. If you can rock the thicc fit, then great, but I’ve gotten some pointed stares when I walk around with them.

The compute puck can be used as a trackpad to navigate the interface, and it also has a fingerprint sensor.

It has been revealed that the glasses do feel lightweight, but after a few minutes of use, they start to heat up. When I take them off, they leave red divots on the bridge of my nose. It’s a small price to pay, though, and it doesn’t ruin the experience. Compare that to something like a VR headset, which does offer better immersion but at the cost of being heavy and uncomfortable to wear for long stretches.

Sources indicate that the compute puck can be an annoyance. It’s light enough, but using the Aura glasses means you have to carry yet another thing that is strapped to the device on your face. There were some smart choices made on the puck, like a fingerprint sensor for biometric authentication, and the puck’s surface works like a trackpad to move the onscreen cursor. That seems much smoother than reaching out to control the device with hand movements, but the trackpad wasn't very precise either. Which is a shame, as it would be ideal for someone on an airplane, say, who wants to control the device without punching the seat in front of them.

In a recent development, controls are the biggest problem I’ve had with the Aura. The front cameras track your hand movements. Hold out your hand and pinch two fingers together to open up an app or move a window. It works most of the time, but some gestures don’t always register. I find myself trying to open Spotify or switch between titles on Prime Video and have to repeatedly pinch the air in front of me for anything to happen. When people have been around to see me, they’ve told me I look like I’ve gone bonkers, just grunting and wildly pinching thin air.

It has been revealed that the Xreal Aura glasses are a stunning display of how far smart-glasses technology has come. But they still feel like a novelty that most people won’t want or need. They haven’t quite solved the core issues facing the product category—looking like a dork or being effortlessly comfortable to wear. But they do feel like a big step in the right direction. If only they could get a pinch more usable.

5 important Bose headphone settings that need to be manually turned on

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (931 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pairing your Bose headphones is just the beginning.
  • Bose has made some of the most popular headphones around for years, but even if you've been using them for a while, you may not be getting everything you can out of yours.
  • It has been revealed that keep in mind that not every pair of Bose headphones will have access to all of these settings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pairing your Bose headphones is just the beginning. A few small tweaks in the companion app's settings can make your headphones feel more like yours.

Bose has made some of the most popular headphones around for years, but even if you've been using them for a while, you may not be getting everything you can out of yours. The tech giant's headphones are perfectly capable of producing great sound right out of the box, but some of their best features actually have to be activated manually. Whether there's something you always wished your headphones could do or you just want to see if they can perform even better, it's worth exploring settings like an equalizer, multi-connection support, noise canceling, shortcuts to your favorite features, or sidetone settings.

It has been revealed that keep in mind that not every pair of Bose headphones will have access to all of these settings. Newer QuietComfort models are upgraded in all the right places, offering a few unique features, while first-generation QuietComfort Ultra and QuietComfort headphones lack some of those features. You'll also need to download the Bose app to tweak anything beyond their basic settings, as the controls on the headphones themselves are pretty minimal.

Industry observers note that one useful feature on compatible Bose headphones is the equalizer (EQ). Like with any piece of audio equipment, the equalizer lets you modify different sound frequencies to your taste, like adjusting the audio quality in Apple Music, letting you pump up the bass or improving the high end so it's brighter. Reviews often call out Bose for boosting bass too much out of the box, so it may be a good idea to try turning it down a touch before making other adjustments.

Bose's equalizer only lets you change volume across three bands — bass, mid and treble — but that's plenty for most users without making it too complex. There are also preset options to choose from if you want to take Bose's recommendations or pick one to start with and customize your profile from there. You'll find the equalizer on the home screen of the Bose app, under EQ.

One of the more annoying aspects of using Bluetooth headphones is having to disconnect and reconnect them whenever you want to switch from one device to another. Bluetooth multipoint lets Bluetooth devices connect to multiple sources at once, so you can switch between them without disconnecting and reconnecting. Compatible Bose headphones have this feature, but you have to enable it in the app.

You'll find Bluetooth multipoint in the Settings section of the app, under Bluetooth Connections. Just toggle it on, and you'll be able to connect your headphones to two different audio sources. To switch devices, pause the audio on one and press play on the other, or swap between them in the app if the switch doesn't happen. Like basically everything to do with Bluetooth, multipoint connection doesn't always work perfectly, but it's extremely convenient when it does.

Bose features some serious pros of using noise-canceling headphones. You can choose from a few modes to adjust how noise-canceling works, with newer models adding more modes. QuietComfort Ultra headphones turn on in Quiet mode by default, but if you find an option you like better, you can set the app to remember the last mode used through the app's Settings menu.

Sources indicate that under the Modes menu in the app, you'll find at least two different noise-canceling presets, depending on which headphones you have. Quiet (full noise cancellation) and Aware (full transparency) are available on the QuietComfort Ultra headphones. In newer headphones, Immersion mode aims to replicate the experience of music being played from a stage in front of you, and Cinema mode enhances dialogue clarity while you're watching movies and TV. You can also define multiple custom modes by choosing which specific noise-canceling features to activate.

Many Bose headphones let you customize their controls, though the specifics will obviously depend on which model you own. QuietComfort Ultra headphones have a touch-sensitive strip, and older headphone models offer the Action Button, both of which can activate your chosen shortcut.

To set the behavior of the custom control, check the Shortcut option in the app. Depending on your model, this will let you choose from a few options, including hearing the battery level as it changes, changing the Immersive Audio mode and switching between previously connected Bluetooth devices. For headphones, you can only set one, but some earbuds let you assign a different shortcut to each ear. If you don't use shortcuts and don't want to risk accidentally activating them, you can also turn them off completely in the app.

According to recent reports, A somewhat more niche feature comes in the form of Self Voice. If you've ever taken a call while wearing headphones, especially noise-canceling ones, you might be familiar with how strange it can be to hear your own voice muffled as you speak. By default, Bose headphones feed a certain amount of your own voice back to you to make speaking feel more natural, otherwise known as sidetone.

In a recent development, the Self Voice feature in the app lets you adjust just how much comes through, but you won't find it on the home screen. Instead, tap the Settings gear icon and look for Self Voice there, where you can set it to High, Medium or Low, or turn it off completely. As long as it's not turned off, Self Voice activates automatically during calls, so you don't need to manually toggle it on.

It has been revealed that we all kind of want to be Tony Stark, don’t we? Almost everyone can relate to that futuristic sense of wonder that comes from the movies where we see digital elements being interacted with through a simple wave of the hand. To date, that’s only really been replicable through major ol’ headsets like Apple’s Vision Pro or the various Meta Quest sets. But with XREAL Aura, Android XR brings that feeling to something far easier to actually use, but my one remaining question is who this product is for.

Industry observers note that XREAL isn’t new to the mixed reality space. The company has been building some of the best example of optical see-through XR glasses. These aren’t quite like a VR headset because they actually let you see the world around you, not through a camera, but by simply making the lenses themselves see-through. I’ve tried these in the past and, while they’re great for mirroring a tablet or laptop for bigger screen (especially on airplanes), I did feel they were missing something.

But first, let’s talk hardware.

XREAL Aura is a two-part device. There are the glasses themselves which include two displays, one for each eye, and electrochromic dimming on the lenses to control just how much of the outer world you’re seeing. It’s wildly different from a typical VR headset, while also having most of the same benefits. Unlike most other XREAL glasses, Aura has built-in world-facing cameras used for hand and spatial tracking, as well as being able to be used as a camera for things like scanning QR codes, Gemini Live, or simply taking a quick picture (there’s no privacy light here, but the bulkier-than-normal design compared to standard glasses is more than enough a dead giveaway that the “perv glasses” dilemma doesn’t really apply in my opinion).

The other half of the formula is a wired puck that provides battery power and the brains of Android XR. There’s no screen on the puck, just a status light, and it has USB-C out for the glasses as well as USB-C in for power and/or external devices. It also has a fingerprint sensor (are you hearing this Android tablet makers??) and a touchpad, the latter used as a secondary, far subtler input method within Android XR to supplement hand tracking.

According to recent reports, together, these two make a wonderful package for building a true mixed reality experience. The displays are plenty bright for even the brightest indoor conditions (frankly, it’d be insane to use these outside in my opinion, though a wide-open plane window may present a challenge), and the electrochromic dimming does a great job of blocking out most, but not quite all of the world around you. If you’re looking to be fully cut off from reality as you would with a VR headset, these aren’t for you. I did find some display elements, like smaller text, a little tough to focus my eyes on at times, but I have a feeling that’s more so me being overdue for an eye exam than it is the glasses themselves. There’s virtually no flicker in my usage, with only bright white backgrounds occasionally being a little overbearing, and everything is smooth with the 120Hz refresh rate.

Where this hardware really shines compared to a typical VR headset is in its design, and it’s what makes XREAL a perfect partner for Android XR. The glasses themselves weigh in at 95 grams, a mere fifth of the Meta Quest 3 and Samsung’s Galaxy XR, and up to 700 grams less than Apple’s Vision Pro. It’s comfortable for much longer periods of time and not nearly as annoying to actually put on either, as it just feels like putting on a pair of bulky sunglasses. They look a little goofy, obviously, but far less so than a full-on VR headset like any of those mentioned above. This is also the only one of those I consider “mixed reality” thanks to the see-through lenses. Apple and Samsung constantly talk about Vision Pro and Galaxy XR as if they’re mixed reality, but a camera feed is explicitly not true reality. But XREAL’s glasses still aren’t quite just augmented reality, because they’re not just letting you see that digital world through a tiny window, they’re quite literally overlaying everything on top of the real world around you. The illusion is somewhat broken by the limited 70-degree field-of-view and the fact that darker backgrounds often look a little funky when there are light sources in the real world in front of you, but I can say with confidence that this is my favorite version of this experience – the speakers are pretty good too, topping it all off.

And that brings us to Android XR.

Google’s platform launched on Samsung’s Galaxy XR headset earlier this year, and it’s all pretty familiar on XREAL Aura. The Android-based experience opens up to a floating launcher of your favorite apps that mostly open up into floating windows in front of you. You can use hand gestures to move everything around or interact with UI elements, and every app I tried worked perfectly well. The gestures can be hit or miss at times, especially the one for going back to the home screen (having this as a long-press that you have to physically look at your hand for gets annoying when doing anything remotely fast-paced, but thankfully the top button is a dedicated home shortcut), but it works well and everything is designed fairly intuitively. A floating cursor demonstrates where you are aiming with a pinch acting as a tap on a touchscreen, and you can move things around in your space as if they’re real objects. There’s a sense of depth throughout the entire experience.

Recent findings suggest that some apps open to fully immersive experiences, but these are still in the minority. XREAL touts that there are around 150 experiences launching alongside Aura, but it’s definitely still early days here. Apps like Google TV should obviously be ready for a full format like that but, most things, like the Google Docs app which I’m typing this review in right now, just act as if they’re on independent displays floating around you.

Like Googlebook, Android XR is also still struggling to figure out the best app experience for each user. Most things are mobile apps, including Google Chrome which is just the standard Android version from your phone. It’s fine in most cases, but I found this restrictive seeing as I can get a ton done in a browser, but fighting mobile optimization is a frustrating way to interact with a window that can be as major as a TV if you want it to. Meanwhile, the Spotify app is weirdly the web version which is horribly optimized for interacting with hand gestures. I’d have rather had the mobile version here. Another quirk I found was notifications, which pop up at the top of the display and quite literally on top of whatever you’re doing. Something they were invasive, and having to physically reach out to dismiss them is a little annoying. I’m sure there are workflows to help make this less of a distraction, but I’d almost rather have notifications turned off entirely.

Industry observers note that there’s also Gemini, which is core to the experience here. A quick “Hey Google” triggers a Gemini Live session for answering questions, and you can share what you’re seeing to give additional context. It’s way faster than switching between apps to get a quick search done, but there are friction points here, especially if you’re just asking a single question. Gemini answers quickly and leaves the conversation going, great for follow-up queries, bad if you’re done because the UI controls go away, which leaves you to tell Gemini to end the session which, every time, it asks for secondary confirmation you want to end. Google, if I say “end the session,” I think that should be more than sufficient proof I want to end the session. Luckily, a long-press of the top home button fixes that headache, but I still hate that I either need to use a physical control, or basically have to fight an AI to end a conversation that I started hands-free.

In a recent development, performance is excellent. Everything is smooth and quick, probably thanks in part to XREAL’s use of 12GB of RAM alongside Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Reality Elite chip.

But how do you actually use a product like this?

That’s the question I found myself asking when I first spun up XREAL Aura and started to learn its ins and outs. See, other XREAL glasses have an extremely straightforward use case. Plug in the external device of your choice, get it on a bigger screen. Simple, easy, obvious. I found this helpful in travel primarily, with a bigger display for my MacBook feeling nice for tasks like video editing, while the main value came in just having a very comfortable way to watch a movie on a flight from my connected tablet.

In a recent development, both of those use cases are valid on XREAL Aura. You can plug a USB-C device into the puck to get that wired mirroring through an Android XR window, and it works super well. Having Android XR alongside that mirroring also opens the door to added functionality, like having extra windows off to the side for perhaps a media app or reference document if you run out of room on the wired device. As just one example, I kept Spotify and Slack open in side windows while using Aura with my MacBook Air for an afternoon of writing articles.

I think Android XR makes Aura an absolute powerhouse for media consumption, as you can just download content directly to the device (256GB of storage in the base model) for a flight, or even just use streaming apps if you have Wi-Fi. I couldn’t find any 3D content during my brief review period (nothing in my Google TV library was compatible, apparently), but that’s also on the table. Genuinely, I cannot wait to use these on my next long flight.

But outside of those, I think a lot of the other scenarios start to fall apart.

By far the most popular use case for virtual/mixed reality has been gaming. XREAL Aura has a ton of potential here and I’m really excited to try out Project Hail Mary: Journey to the Stars on this, but the fact that these are simply glasses restricts a lot of what you can do. Any big movements could easily result in the glasses slipping or even falling off, whereas a VR headset is much more secure. Stationary immersive gaming has potential, and XREAL’s Gamesir controller collab reveals promise, but I’m just not sold on these as a replacement to something like Meta Quest seeing as the latter already has a deep catalog of games and a much more affordable price.

The other use case is productivity, one I’m also not entirely sold on. As mentioned, this entire post was written in Aura, and I’m not sure I benefitted much from that experience versus just using a normal laptop or desktop computer. My workflow was having Google Docs up in the center, typing on a physical keyboard (only a psycho could use the virtual keyboard for anything beyond the shortest messages or passwords) with reference documents in Chrome off to my right and Slack on my left, with the occasional “Hey Google” command helping to find information on the fly (such as the weight comparison earlier). It all works well, but I think Android XR is inherently limited by its reliance mostly on mobile apps, and also just by the use of gestures. You can use a mouse or trackpad, of course, but at that point you might as well just use a laptop.

According to recent reports, XREAL Aura is for a very specific customer from my point of view. Wired mirroring is still very much the strong suit here, with Android XR’s apps and offline video giving these utility outside of just relying on another device. That was my problem with previous XREAL glasses, because the experience just varies wildly depending on what’s connected. Aura’s puck and Android XR experience solves every complaint I had about previous models, while expanding very much on what it can do.

According to recent reports, further limiting matters is the price. $1,279, in my book, is actually a mostly fair price for this, especially given the RAMageddon of it all. XREAL 1+ Pro come in around $600 and is utterly useless without a secondary device. XREAL Aura more or less doubles the price, but includes the best possible version of that secondary device while also giving you the added camera sensors that are only available as add-ons for other hardware. Don’t get me wrong, it’s still pricey, but I don’t think it’s unfair either, especially not when one of the main competitors for this sort of experience is still $3,600 (which still sounds insane two years later, even for Apple).

In a recent development, we’ll have far more to say about XREAL Aura in a long-term review from our Nick Sutrich, but the verdict on day one is that Android XR has really solved the biggest problem for XREAL, while XREAL has solved a lot of big problems for Android XR, all while being an overall win for the user at the end of the day. Not so often we get a storybook ending like that in tech anymore, and I’m all here for it.

Recent findings suggest that don’t forget, XREAL Aura is $200 off – so $1,099 – through the end of December. Much more worth it at that price.

Science Corporation’s brain tech is worth $3.5 billion after new funding

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Science Corporation, the medical technology start-up founded by former Neuralink president Max Hodak in 2021, raised a $400 million Series D, the company noted in a blog post.

Sources indicate that investors in the new round valued the organization at $3.5 billion, a person familiar with the deal told TechCrunch. Those backers included Khosla Ventures, the Ackman Oxman Institute, Tenet Healthcare, 885 Capital, Y Combinator, and PLC Neurotech.

Hodak, who talked his way into a graduate neuroscience lab as a college student and has pursued biotechnology ever since, co-founded Science to leverage latest technologies to understand and interact with the brain.

Recent findings suggest that science’s first product is PRIMA, a wearable and implantable chip that helps people with age-related macular degeneration recover some vision. The device is approved in Europe and available in Germany, as well as being trialled for new conditions.

Hodak announced that the device is now being trialled for patients with another blindness-causing condition, Stargardt’s disease, while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt.

Recent findings suggest that with the funding, the company aims to bring the device to the United States through the FDA’s Humanitarian Device Exemption, which lets experimental medical technology be used to treat rare conditions. Science has convinced the FDA that advanced macular degeneration in both eyes is uncommon enough to let them seek approval to use the device on people in the US.

It has been revealed that still, the startup’s big ambition and founding purpose is connecting directly to the human brain through a bio-hybrid sensor built from a combination of cultured neurons and silicon. The manufacturer is right now designing initial human trials of the device with Yale neurosurgery professor Murat Günel, who told TechCrunch it could offer potential treatments for Parkinson’s disease, among other brain injuries and illnesses.
